result:
I’ve always found the concept of liminal spaces deeply fascinating—not just the abandoned, echoing shopping malls or midnight gas stations of internet folklore, but the literal, microscopic thresholds that exist in every given second. 

Right now, as you read this, you are technically traveling through time. You are sitting on a planet hurtling through space at roughly 67,000 miles per hour, orbiting a star that is dragging our entire solar system through the Milky Way. And yet, the most profound thing happening in your immediate vicinity might just be the quiet rhythm of your own breathing, or the gentle weight of gravity keeping your cup of coffee on the desk. 

I love the paradox of scale. How we can be so infinitesimally small—a pale blue dot, a fleeting organization of carbon and water—yet so profoundly important to the micro-universes we carry with us. To a dust mite, a living room rug is an endless, sprawling forest. To the bacteria in your gut, you are a walking, breathing galaxy. 

I think we forget to look up. Or, perhaps more accurately, we forget to look *closely*. 

When was the last time you looked at a solid object—say, a wooden table—and really thought about the fact that it is mostly empty space? That the atoms comprising it are separated by vast, relative distances, bound together by invisible forces? That the wood was once a living, breathing tree, drinking sunlight and filtering the air? That the finish on it might be the compressed ghosts of prehistoric ferns? 

Sometimes I think the human brain evolved specifically to ignore the terrifying, magnificent complexity of reality. If we truly comprehended the miracle of physics and chemistry occurring in the simple act of a seed sprouting, or a fire burning, or a memory forming in our synapses, we would be too paralyzed by awe to go to work or do the laundry. 

We are built for routine. But every so often, the veil drops. You hear a specific song, or you catch the light filtering through the autumn leaves at the exact right angle, and for a split second, you remember that you are a piece of the universe that has briefly gained consciousness. You are stardust contemplating stardust.

We get so caught up in the torrent of human drama—our anxieties, our deadlines, our endless scrolling through digital feeds—that we mistake the map for the territory. We forget that the screen you are looking at, the eyes you are looking with, and the mind processing the words are all miraculous anomalies of physics. 

It’s a strange, beautiful, heavy thing, being alive. There is no manual for it, no right way to do it. We are all just improvising on a floating rock, trying to figure out how to be kind, how to find meaning, and how to marvel at the sheer, unlikeliness of it all before the lights go out. 

I suppose, if I am writing freely about whatever I want, what I really want to say is this: I hope you find a moment today to pause. I hope you let the sheer improbability of your own existence catch you off guard, just for a second, and I hope it makes you smile.
